claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes the selected high-entropy alloy as a single phase.
The single-phase alloy has a disordered but spatially uniform lattice.
A disordered but uniform lattice promotes effective electron-phonon coupling and thereby enables robust superconductivity.
Disrupting lattice homogeneity through phase separation diminishes superconductivity.
The as-cast starting alloy has a random, well-mixed elemental distribution.
The as-cast starting alloy forms a single bcc or CsCl-type phase.
Annealing can reduce configurational disorder and promote phase separation in the selected alloy.
The proposed measurements are to be performed below the expected critical temperature under ambient to moderate pressure.
High configurational entropy mediates a uniform lattice parameter and single-phase structure.
A uniform single-phase lattice minimizes local inhomogeneities.
The homogeneous high-entropy structure reduces spatial variability in electron scattering.
The homogeneous high-entropy structure enhances electron-phonon interactions.
Enhanced electron-phonon interaction favors consistent Cooper-pair formation despite compositional disorder.
The as-cast high-entropy state will exhibit a clear superconducting transition.
The transition will appear as a sharp resistivity drop and a diamagnetic susceptibility response.
The alloy's critical temperature will be relatively insensitive to moderate pressure changes.
Annealed, phase-separated samples will have a diminished or absent superconducting signature relative to the as-cast state.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single phase and may change or vanish after secondary phases form.
The exact critical temperature and critical-field robustness are uncertain because precedent for comparable uncharacterized high-entropy superconductors is limited.

contradictions.description: The intervention and comparison require an annealed group with intentional phase separation, while the conditions state that the alloy should remain within its single-phase boundary. The latter cannot apply simultaneously to the intended phase-separated comparison group.
